with-the-173rd.summary: A single Australian battalion fights under American command in Bien Hoa province, first guarding the air base, then on operations further afield.
with-the-173rd.text:
By early 1965 it had become clear that South Vietnam could not hold off the communist insurgents and their North Vietnamese allies for long, and the United States began a major build-up of its forces, asking its allies to help[1]. Australia sent the 1st Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment (1 RAR), which arrived between March and June 1965 and served as the third battalion of the US 173rd Airborne Brigade at Bien Hoa Air Base, in Bien Hoa province[1][2].

At first the battalion was confined to defending the air base; in September 1965 the Australian government lifted that restriction, and 1 RAR went out on operations with the Americans[2]. Among them were Operation Crimp in the Hobo Woods north of Saigon in January 1966, where it uncovered part of the Cu Chi tunnel complex, and Operation Rolling Stone in February, guarding US engineers building a road[2].

The record holds 461 contacts from this year, 430 of them 1 RAR's. They show a mixed kind of war: 129 were recorded as patrols, 104 as security of installations, 45 as sightings and 42 as harassing fire, with 30 mines or booby traps. Most operations are numbered rather than named in the record (10/65, 12/65, 1/66); the largest named ones were Silver City, in March 1966, and Abilene. The record counts 19 killed and 89 wounded on the allied side, and 118 enemy killed.

The battalion's patrols and security work cut enemy activity around the air base to an all-time low[2]. But the Australian government wanted a contribution that was both larger and clearly Australian, able to fight in its own way and under its own command, and in March 1966 it announced a task force of two battalions to replace 1 RAR, with its own province[1][3].

sources.title: Nui Dat base in Phuoc Tuy Province during the Vietnam War

establishing-nui-dat.summary: The 1st Australian Task Force arrives in Phuoc Tuy, builds its base at Nui Dat in the middle of Viet Cong country, and clears the villages around it.
establishing-nui-dat.text:
The Task Force was approved on 8 March 1966[1]. Phuoc Tuy province, on the coast south-east of Saigon, was chosen for it: a province of the right size, with a port at Vung Tau for supplies, where the South Vietnamese government held little more than the capital, Ba Ria, and the Viet Cong ran the countryside, with perhaps 5,000 troops and bases in the hills and jungle[1].

The base was built at Nui Dat, 'small hill', in the centre of the province: away from the towns but close to the Viet Cong's base areas, and so right in their territory[1]. To secure it, everyone living within about 4 kilometres of a line around the base, Line Alpha, was moved out. In Operation Hardihood, from May, 5 RAR, 1 RAR and the US 173rd Airborne cleared the villages of Long Phuoc and Long Tan and resettled their people at Hoa Long, Dat Do and Long Dien[1]. The resettlement, without compensation, made the base safer but set back efforts to win the people's support[1]. In June and July, after mortar attacks on the base continued, 6 RAR searched and destroyed the empty village of Long Phuoc in Operation Enoggera[1].

The record holds 246 contacts in these months, most of them 5 RAR's (117) and, from June, 6 RAR's (68), with the Special Air Service's first patrols. Half were recorded as patrols (125), and the rest mostly security (34) and ambushes (23). Hardihood alone accounts for 88. The Task Force recorded 11 of its own killed, three of the contacts as friendly fire, and 83 enemy killed.

sources.title: Nui Dat base in Phuoc Tuy Province during the Vietnam War

long-tan-and-the-province.summary: The enemy tests the new base at Long Tan, and the two battalions then push out across the province to cordon villages and search the hills.
long-tan-and-the-province.text:
On 18 August 1966, three months after the base was set up, D Company of 6 RAR met a far larger force in the rubber plantation at Long Tan, close to the Task Force's base at Nui Dat[1]. The resettlement of Long Tan and Long Phuoc was a reason for the attack on the Task Force[1]. Captured documents and prisoners suggested some 2,500 enemy, among them the Viet Cong 275th Main Force Regiment, at least one North Vietnamese battalion and the local D445 Battalion[1]. The record counts 17 Australians killed and 245 enemy killed in that one contact.

Afterwards the Task Force widened its grip on the province. The record's contacts from these months (290 of them) are mostly patrols (151), with security (39) and ambushes (26). The operations were cordons and searches of villages, such as Holsworthy at Binh Ba in August, which rooted out the Viet Cong's organisation there for a time, and searches of the enemy's base areas, such as Vaucluse, in the Nui Dinh hills in September, and Ingham in November, a 'search and destroy' operation and the largest of these months, with 37 contacts[2][3][4]. The armoured personnel carriers of the 3rd Cavalry Regiment and the Special Air Service appear more often in the record (33 and 31 contacts).

In all, the record counts 45 killed on the Task Force's side and 140 wounded in these months, and 429 enemy killed.

the-barrier-minefield.summary: A second rotation of battalions arrives, and the Task Force tries to seal off the populated south with a fence and a belt of mines.
the-barrier-minefield.text:
The first two battalions went home in May and June 1967, and 2 RAR and 7 RAR took their place. With only two battalions to cover the province, the Task Force commander, Brigadier Stuart Graham, looked for a way to multiply their strength[1]. The answer was a barrier: a fence and a belt of more than 20,000 mines across the south of the province[1]. Its purpose was to safeguard the rice harvest and to cut the enemy's main forces off from the villages of the south, easing the patrolling the Task Force could not keep up[1].

The barrier was meant to be watched by Australian patrols on one side and South Vietnamese on the other, but it was not protected, and the Viet Cong went to great lengths to recover its mines and lay them again against the Australians[1]. The historian Greg Lockhart argues that people from the nearby villages lifted thousands of them, and that from late 1967 to early 1971 they were the enemy's main weapon in the province[3]. The Task Force also moved villagers again that year, to Suoi Nghe[1].

This is the busiest year yet in the record: 932 contacts. They include a great many recorded against the artillery of 4th Field Regiment (176), with 7 RAR (110) and 2 RAR (78) the infantry most often in contact. Of those with a task recorded, patrols led (168), then security (77) and ambushes (62). The operations were many and short, the largest Santa Fe (49 contacts) and Forrest (43), at the year's end. The record counts 36 killed on the Task Force's side and 118 wounded, and 235 enemy killed. In December a third battalion, 3 RAR, arrived[2].

tet-and-beyond-the-province.summary: With a third battalion and tanks, the Task Force is sent beyond Phuoc Tuy for the first time, as the Tet offensive strikes the towns and Saigon.
tet-and-beyond-the-province.text:
In early 1968 the North Vietnamese and Viet Cong struck in the Tet holiday, attacking as many towns and bases as they could at once, in the hope of provoking a general uprising against the South Vietnamese government[1]. There was no uprising, and the offensive was a military defeat for the communists, but its scale shook American resolve and turned opinion around the world[1][2].

For the first time, the Task Force was sent out of Phuoc Tuy: from 24 January to 1 March, 2 RAR and 7 RAR, with armour, artillery and engineers, took part in Operation Coburg on the Bien Hoa–Long Khanh border, protecting allied bases during the offensive[3]. The record has 142 contacts from Coburg. At home, the Viet Cong's D445 Battalion seized Ba Ria on 1 February; 3 RAR, carried in the 3rd Cavalry Regiment's armoured personnel carriers, fought to clear it, and a week later helped the South Vietnamese clear Long Dien[1]. The first tanks, of the 1st Armoured Regiment, arrived in February.

From March, 3 RAR, with armoured personnel carriers and tanks, was in Operation Pinnaroo (80 contacts). Then in May the Task Force went north again, to intercept enemy forces moving to and from Saigon: fire support bases Coral and Balmoral, in Operation Toan Thang, held against attacks by North Vietnamese battalions between 12 May and 6 June, the Australians' most costly and protracted battle of the war[4]. The record's 144 contacts for Toan Thang 1 count 29 Australians killed.

These six months hold 717 contacts, with 63 recorded killed on the Task Force's side and 328 wounded, and 718 enemy killed: the heaviest fighting of the war so far.

sources.title: Tet Offensive, Operation Coburg and the Battle of Ba Ria 1968

across-the-region.summary: Three battalions work across the region as much as the province: long operations in Bien Hoa and Long Khanh, then back to Phuoc Tuy.
across-the-region.text:
After Coral and Balmoral the Task Force was often used beyond its own province. The largest of these operations was Goodwood, from 3 December 1968 to 19 February 1969, in Bien Hoa, Long Khanh and Phuoc Tuy provinces[1]; 9 RAR, which had arrived in November to relieve 3 RAR, joined it on 1 January, as signs grew that the enemy was planning an offensive, and afterwards searched and patrolled there in Operation Federal after the 1969 Tet offensive[2].

The record shows how much work this year held: 1,304 contacts, more than any year before. Goodwood alone has 257 of them, and Federal 84. With Goodwood, Lavarack (83) and Overlander (62) were the year's largest. Patrols (493) and ambushes (327) were now the bulk of it, with security (240). 9 RAR (231), 4 RAR (157), 5 RAR (155) and 1 RAR (150) were most often in contact.

From April 1969 the battalions' work turned towards pacification: seeking out the enemy in its base areas and keeping him from the people[2]. In June, at Binh Ba, less than 10 kilometres from Nui Dat, the Task Force's ready reaction company, with armoured personnel carriers and tanks, helped South Vietnamese forces retake the village from North Vietnamese and Viet Cong troops in two days of fighting (Operation Hammer)[3].

The record counts 85 killed on the Task Force's side and 488 wounded in the year, and 1,073 enemy killed.

sources.title: Australians in the Battle of Binh Ba 6 to 7 June 1969

pacification.summary: As the Americans begin to withdraw, the Task Force works to keep the enemy from the people and to hand the province's security to the South Vietnamese.
pacification.text:
In 1969 the United States began Vietnamisation: a gradual withdrawal of its forces, leaving the war to the South Vietnamese[1]. In Phuoc Tuy the Task Force's emphasis shifted accordingly, towards training the South Vietnamese Regional and Popular Forces, the province's own troops[1]. The battalions' work was pacification: seeking out and destroying the enemy in its base areas, keeping him away from the villages, and helping to create a secure climate for the South Vietnamese[2].

This is the longest and busiest stretch in the record: 1,721 contacts in 17 months. Patrols (515) and ambushes (416) make up more than half of those with a task, with security (308); the big set-piece operation gave way to many smaller ones, the largest Kings Cross (85 contacts), Concrete (63) and Napier (60). From June 1970 Operation Cung Chung set battalions to intensive patrolling and ambushing to deter the enemy from moving through the area[2]. 5 RAR (228), 6 RAR (212) and 8 RAR (211) were most often in contact, with the units under the Task Force's headquarters (195) and the 3rd Cavalry Regiment (152).

Mines were the great danger of these years; the historian Greg Lockhart argues that until early 1971 the mines lifted from the Task Force's own barrier field were the enemy's main weapon in the province[3]. The record counts 96 killed on the Task Force's side and 671 wounded in these months, and 967 enemy killed. By late 1970 Australia too had begun to wind down: 8 RAR left in November and was not replaced[1].

the-withdrawal.summary: Down to two battalions, the Task Force holds the province while it prepares to leave, and fights one last major action at Nui Le.
the-withdrawal.text:
From December 1970 the Task Force had two battalions, not three[1]. To make up for fewer troops, more Australian advisers were sent to train the South Vietnamese, and their work was concentrated in Phuoc Tuy[1]. In February 1971 3 RAR relieved 7 RAR[2], and in May 4 RAR relieved 2 RAR.

The record's 485 contacts from these months show the change: for the first time ambushes (130) outnumber patrols (108), with security (106), and the 3rd Cavalry Regiment's armoured personnel carriers (92 contacts) are in the record as often as any battalion. Phoi Hop (73 contacts), Briar Patch (64) and the last months of Cung Chung 3 (59) were the largest.

In September 1971, with parts of the Task Force already going home, the North Vietnamese 33rd Regiment tried to establish itself in Phuoc Tuy[3]. The Task Force commander chose to stop it, knowing that Australian lives would be lost as the Task Force was about to withdraw[3]. In Operation Ivanhoe, led by 4 RAR, the battle at Nui Le on 21 September cost 6 Australians killed and 29 wounded[3]. The last battalion left Nui Dat on 7 November 1971[1].

The record counts 34 killed on the Task Force's side and 158 wounded in the Task Force's last year, and 262 enemy killed.

sources.title: Operation Ivanhoe and the Battle of Nui Le 1971
